questions.stem: In CPU scheduling, the **response time** of a process is best defined as the time from
options: its submission (arrival) until its completion
its arrival until it is first given the CPU
its arrival until its last CPU burst begins
the moment it is dispatched until it completes
questions.explanation: Response time = (time of first CPU allocation) − (arrival time). It measures how quickly a process *starts* getting service, which matters for interactive systems. Arrival-to-completion is turnaround time; total time spent in the ready queue is waiting time.
option_feedback: That is turnaround time.
Correct: arrival to the first time the process gets the CPU.
Not a standard criterion; response time is about the *first* allocation.
Dispatch-to-completion ignores the time spent waiting before the first dispatch.

questions.stem: A CPU scheduler is designed to optimise the usual criteria. Which one of the following should be **maximised** (not minimised)?
options: Average waiting time
Average turnaround time
Average response time
Throughput
questions.explanation: Throughput = number of processes completed per unit time, so we want it as large as possible (likewise CPU utilisation). Waiting time, turnaround time and response time are all delays and are minimised.
option_feedback: Waiting time is a delay — minimise it.
Turnaround time is a delay — minimise it.
Response time is a delay — minimise it.
Correct: throughput (jobs completed per unit time) is maximised.

questions.stem: A process arrives at time 3, needs a single CPU burst of 5 ms and does no I/O. It completes at time 17. Ignoring context-switch time, its waiting time (in ms) is ______.
questions.explanation:
Turnaround time = completion − arrival = 17 − 3 = 14 ms.
Waiting time = turnaround − burst = 14 − 5 = **9 ms** (time spent in the ready queue).
questions.trap: Subtracting the burst from the completion time (17 − 5 = 12) forgets the arrival time.

questions.stem: Assume a continuous stream of new processes may keep arriving. Which of the following scheduling algorithms can cause **starvation** (indefinite postponement) of a ready process?
options: First-Come-First-Served
Non-preemptive Shortest Job First
Round Robin
Preemptive priority scheduling without aging
questions.explanation:
- **SJF** keeps choosing the shortest job; a long job can be bypassed forever if short jobs keep arriving.
- **Priority** (preemptive or not) without aging can postpone a low-priority process indefinitely.
- **FCFS** serves in arrival order: every process eventually reaches the head of the queue.
- **Round Robin** bounds the wait: with n processes and quantum q, a process waits at most (n − 1)·q before its next turn.
option_feedback: FCFS is starvation-free: later arrivals are always behind you.
Correct: short jobs can bypass a long job forever.
RR gives everyone a turn within (n − 1)·q.
Correct: without aging a low-priority process may never run.

questions.stem: A system runs only CPU-bound processes (no I/O) under Round Robin with time quantum 12 ms. Every context switch costs 3 ms, and there are always at least two ready processes, so a switch follows every quantum. The CPU utilisation (useful work as a percentage of total time) is ______ %.
questions.explanation:
Each cycle = one full quantum of useful work + one switch = 12 + 3 = 15 ms.
Utilisation = 12 / 15 = 0.8 = **80 %**.
questions.trap: Using s/q or q/(q − s) instead of q/(q + s).

questions.stem: Each process in a system spends 80 % of its time waiting for I/O. Assume the processes behave independently, so the CPU is idle only when all of them are waiting for I/O simultaneously. With 4 such processes in memory, the CPU utilisation is ______ % (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
P(one process is waiting for I/O) = p = 0.8.
P(all 4 waiting) = 0.8⁴ = 0.4096 → CPU idle 40.96 % of the time.
CPU utilisation = 1 − 0.8⁴ = 0.5904 = **59.04 %**.
questions.trap: Computing 4 × 20 % = 80 % ignores overlap between the processes' CPU phases.

questions.stem: Assume CPU burst lengths are known exactly and context-switch time is zero. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: When all processes arrive at time 0, non-preemptive SJF gives the minimum average waiting time among all schedules.
Non-preemptive SJF always gives the minimum average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules, even when processes arrive at different times.
SRTF gives the minimum average waiting time among all (preemptive or non-preemptive) schedules.
When all processes arrive at time 0, SRTF and non-preemptive SJF produce the same schedule (up to tie-breaking) and the same average waiting time.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: with all jobs present, total waiting = Σ (position weight × burst) is minimised by running shortest first (exchange argument).
- **B** False: with staggered arrivals a non-preemptive scheduler may do better by idling briefly to wait for a short job. Example: P1(AT 0, BT 10), P2(AT 1, BT 1). SJF runs P1 at 0 → WT = 0 + 9, avg 4.5. Idling 1 unit and running P2 first → WT(P1) = 2, WT(P2) = 0, avg 1. So greedy SJF is not optimal among all non-preemptive schedules.
- **C** True: SRTF is the preemptive optimum for average waiting/turnaround time.
- **D** True: if no process arrives later, there is never a shorter newcomer to preempt the running one, so SRTF never preempts and behaves exactly like SJF.
option_feedback: True — the classic SJF optimality result.
False — greedy SJF commits to a long job that a short later arrival could have beaten.
True — shortest remaining time first is optimal for average waiting time.
True — with no later arrivals SRTF never preempts.
questions.trap: Believing SJF is optimal unconditionally; the guarantee needs all jobs available together.

questions.stem: Three processes P1, P2, P3 arrive at time 0 with total execution times 10, 20 and 40 ms respectively. Each process spends the first 30 % of its execution time doing I/O, the next 50 % computing on the CPU, and the last 20 % doing I/O again. Every process has its own I/O device (I/O operations overlap freely). The scheduler is FCFS on the ready queue; ignore context-switch time. The percentage of time for which the CPU remains **idle** (from time 0 until all three finish) is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Phases (I/O, CPU, I/O):

| Process | I/O | CPU | I/O |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 3 | 5 | 2 |
| P2 | 6 | 10 | 4 |
| P3 | 12 | 20 | 8 |

So P1 is ready for the CPU at 3, P2 at 6, P3 at 12.

CPU Gantt chart:
```
| idle | P1 | P2 | P3 | idle |
0      3    8    18   38     46
```

- P1: CPU 3–8, I/O 8–10.
- P2: ready at 6 but CPU busy until 8 → CPU 8–18, I/O 18–22.
- P3: ready at 12 → CPU 18–38, I/O 38–46.

Everything finishes at 46. CPU busy = 5 + 10 + 20 = 35 ms, idle = 3 + 8 = 11 ms.
Idle percentage = 11 / 46 × 100 = **23.91 %**.
questions.trap: Forgetting the idle tail 38–46 while P3 does its final I/O, or measuring only up to 38.

questions.stem:
Four processes are scheduled by **SRTF** (preemptive SJF).

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 7 |
| P2 | 2 | 3 |
| P3 | 3 | 5 |
| P4 | 20 | 2 |

Rules:
- Every dispatch of a process (including the first one at time 0 and one after an idle period) is preceded by a context switch of 1 unit. The scheduler picks the process at the **start** of the switch; a process arriving while a switch is in progress is considered as soon as the switch ends.
- A running process is preempted only by a process with **strictly** smaller remaining time; ties among ready processes go to the earlier arrival.

The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Gantt chart (CS = context switch):
```
| CS | P1 | CS | P2 | CS | P3 | CS | P1 | idle | CS | P4 |
0    1    2    3    6    7    12   13   19     20   21   23
```

- 0–1 switch, P1 runs 1–2. Because of the switch, P1 has executed only **1** unit by t = 2, so its remaining time is 6.
- 2: P2 (3) < 6 → preempt; switch 2–3, P2 runs 3–6.
- 3: P3 (5) arrives exactly as the switch ends; P2 has 3 left → no preemption.
- 6: P2 done. Ready: P1 (6 left), P3 (5) → **P3** is shorter: switch 6–7, P3 7–12.
- 12: switch 12–13, P1 13–19 (done).
- 19–20 idle; P4 arrives at 20: switch 20–21, P4 21–23.

| Process | AT | CT | TAT |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 19 | 19 |
| P2 | 2 | 6 | 4 |
| P3 | 3 | 12 | 9 |
| P4 | 20 | 23 | 3 |

Average TAT = 35 / 4 = **8.75**.

The twist: the switch overhead changes a scheduling *decision*. Without switches P1 would have 5 left at t = 5, tie with P3, and win the tie by earlier arrival.
questions.trap: Forgetting that the first switch delays P1, so P1 appears to have 5 units left at t = 6, wins the tie against P3 and gives 9.00; ignoring the switches entirely gives 6.75.

questions.stem: Consider single-CPU scheduling of processes that each have exactly one CPU burst and do no I/O; context-switch time is zero. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: Under any non-preemptive algorithm, a process's response time equals its waiting time.
Under any algorithm, a process's waiting time equals its turnaround time minus its burst time.
Under any preemptive algorithm, a process's response time equals its waiting time.
For Round Robin, reducing the time quantum never increases the average turnaround time.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: once dispatched a non-preemptive process runs to completion, so all its waiting happens before its first dispatch → WT = RT.
- **B** True: TAT = time spent running + time spent ready; with one CPU burst and no I/O, running time = burst, so WT = TAT − BT.
- **C** False: a preempted process waits again later, so WT ≥ RT, usually strictly (e.g. in RR).
- **D** False: average turnaround is not monotonic in q. Three jobs of 10 units at time 0: q = 10 gives completions 10, 20, 30 (avg 20); q = 1 gives 28, 29, 30 (avg 29).
option_feedback: True — all waiting precedes the only dispatch.
True — with one burst and no I/O this is the definition.
False — preempted processes wait again after their first run.
False — a smaller quantum can increase average turnaround (equal-length jobs).
questions.trap: Assuming a smaller quantum is always better; it improves response time, not necessarily turnaround.

questions.stem:
Three processes are in the ready queue at time 0. Each does CPU → I/O → CPU:

| Process | CPU | I/O | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 2 | 4 | 2 |
| P2 | 3 | 3 | 1 |
| P3 | 1 | 5 | 2 |

The CPU is scheduled FCFS. There is a **single** I/O device, also served FCFS (a process that finishes its CPU burst while the device is busy waits for it). Ignore switching time. CPU utilisation = (total CPU busy time) / (time from 0 until the last process completes).

The initial queue order can be any of the 3! = 6 orders. In how many of these orders is the CPU utilisation **at least 70 %**?
questions.explanation:
Busy time is always 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 11, so utilisation ≥ 70 % ⇔ makespan T ≤ 11 / 0.7 = 15.71, i.e. T ≤ 15.

**Key observation.** The device needs 4 + 3 + 5 = 12 units in total. It starts when the first process finishes its first CPU burst, and in every order the next process's first CPU burst ends before the device frees, so the device then works without a gap. The last process to finish I/O then runs its final CPU burst (the CPU is free by then). Hence

T = (first CPU burst of the first process) + 12 + (final CPU burst of the last process).

| Order | Device schedule | T | Utilisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1, P2, P3 | P1 2–6, P2 6–9, P3 9–14 | 2 + 12 + 2 = 16 | 68.75 % |
| P1, P3, P2 | P1 2–6, P3 6–11, P2 11–14 | 2 + 12 + 1 = 15 | 73.33 % |
| P2, P1, P3 | P2 3–6, P1 6–10, P3 10–15 | 3 + 12 + 2 = 17 | 64.71 % |
| P2, P3, P1 | P2 3–6, P3 6–11, P1 11–15 | 3 + 12 + 2 = 17 | 64.71 % |
| P3, P1, P2 | P3 1–6, P1 6–10, P2 10–13 | 1 + 12 + 1 = 14 | 78.57 % |
| P3, P2, P1 | P3 1–6, P2 6–9, P1 9–13 | 1 + 12 + 2 = 15 | 73.33 % |

Example check (order P3, P1, P2), CPU chart:
```
| P3 | P1 | P2 | P3 | idle | P1 | idle | P2 |
0    1    3    6    8      10   12     13   14
```

Orders with T ≤ 15: (P1, P3, P2), (P3, P1, P2), (P3, P2, P1) → **3**.
questions.trap: Letting the I/O operations overlap (as if each process had its own device) makes every order look much better; or checking only the given order P1, P2, P3, which at 68.75 % just misses the bar.

questions.stem: Which statement about First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) CPU scheduling is correct?
options: It is preemptive: a newly arrived process may take the CPU from the running one.
It requires the length of the next CPU burst to be known in advance.
It always gives the minimum average waiting time.
It is non-preemptive and is implemented with a FIFO ready queue.
questions.explanation: FCFS dispatches processes in arrival order from a FIFO queue; once a process gets the CPU it keeps it until it terminates or blocks for I/O. It needs no burst-length information, and its average waiting time is often poor (convoy effect).
option_feedback: FCFS never preempts.
That is the practical problem of SJF, not FCFS.
That is SJF (when all arrive together); FCFS can be far from optimal.
Correct.

questions.stem: The **convoy effect** in CPU scheduling refers to
options: many short processes waiting behind one long CPU-bound process, lowering CPU and device utilisation
a low-priority process never getting the CPU
processes repeatedly exchanging the CPU without making progress
frequent context switches caused by a very small time quantum
questions.explanation: Under FCFS, a long CPU-bound process holds the CPU while I/O-bound processes queue behind it (their devices idle); then they all rush through the CPU and queue at I/O while the CPU idles. This convoy lowers both CPU and device utilisation and inflates average waiting time.
option_feedback: Correct.
That is starvation.
That resembles livelock, not convoy.
That is RR overhead with a tiny quantum.

questions.stem: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3 with CPU bursts 20, 2 and 5 ms. Under FCFS, the average waiting time (in ms) is ______.
A system has one CPU-bound process with long CPU bursts and several I/O-bound processes with very short CPU bursts. Under FCFS, which outcome is most likely?
options: High CPU utilisation and high I/O-device utilisation at all times
The CPU-bound process starves
I/O devices sit idle while the I/O-bound processes wait behind the CPU-bound process
Average waiting time is the minimum possible
questions.explanation: This is the convoy effect: while the CPU-bound process holds the CPU, the I/O-bound processes finish their I/O and wait in the ready queue, so the devices go idle. When the long process finally does I/O, the short ones run quickly and then block, so the CPU goes idle. Both utilisations suffer.
option_feedback: Utilisation drops under the convoy effect.
FCFS never starves anyone; the CPU-bound process is the one that delays others.
Correct — the convoy effect.
Running long jobs before short ones maximises, not minimises, waiting.

questions.stem:
Under FCFS scheduling (ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 4 |
| P2 | 2 | 6 |
| P3 | 3 | 2 |
| P4 | 7 | 5 |

The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).

Under FCFS scheduling (ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 1 | 3 |
| P2 | 2 | 2 |
| P3 | 9 | 4 |
| P4 | 10 | 1 |

The average waiting time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
The CPU is idle until the first arrival and again between 6 and 9.

Gantt chart:
```
| idle | P1 | P2 | idle | P3 | P4 |
0      1    4    6      9    13   14
```

| Process | AT | BT | CT | TAT = CT − AT | WT = TAT − BT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 0 |
| P2 | 2 | 2 | 6 | 4 | 2 |
| P3 | 9 | 4 | 13 | 4 | 0 |
| P4 | 10 | 1 | 14 | 4 | 3 |

Average WT = (0 + 2 + 0 + 3) / 4 = **1.25**.
questions.trap: Starting P3 at 6 (as if it had arrived) gives negative or wrong waiting times; the CPU must idle until 9.

questions.stem: Four processes are all available at time 0 with CPU bursts P1 = 12, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, P4 = 6. FCFS is used. Let W₁ be the average waiting time if they are queued in the order P1, P2, P3, P4 and W₂ the average waiting time if queued in the order P2, P3, P4, P1. The value of W₁ − W₂ is ______.
questions.explanation:
Order P1, P2, P3, P4:
```
|     P1     | P2 | P3 |  P4  |
0            12   15   18     24
```
WT = 0, 12, 15, 18 → W₁ = 45 / 4 = 11.25.

Order P2, P3, P4, P1:
```
| P2 | P3 |  P4  |     P1     |
0    3    6      12           24
```
WT = 0, 3, 6, 12 → W₂ = 21 / 4 = 5.25.

W₁ − W₂ = **6**. Putting the long job first makes every short job wait behind it (convoy effect).

questions.stem:
Four processes are scheduled FCFS.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 |
| P2 | 1 | 3 |
| P3 | 2 | x |
| P4 | 14 | 2 |

Every dispatch of a process (including the first at time 0 and one after an idle period) is preceded by a context switch of 1 unit. A process's waiting time is turnaround time − burst time (so switch time counts as waiting). x is a positive integer. If the average waiting time is **5.5**, the value of x is ______.
questions.explanation:
The first three dispatches do not depend on x:
```
| CS | P1 | CS | P2 | CS |  P3  |
0    1    6    7    10   11   11 + x
```
WT: P1 = 6 − 0 − 5 = 1, P2 = 10 − 1 − 3 = 6, P3 = (11 + x) − 2 − x = 9. Sum so far = 16.

P4 arrives at 14, so there are two regimes:
- **x ≤ 3:** P3 ends at 11 + x ≤ 14; the CPU idles (or is just free) until 14, then switch 14–15, P4 15–17 → WT(P4) = 1. Average = 17 / 4 = 4.25 — never 5.5.
- **x ≥ 3:** P4 is waiting when P3 ends: switch (11 + x)–(12 + x), P4 ends at 14 + x → WT(P4) = (14 + x) − 14 − 2 = x − 2.

Average 5.5 ⇒ total 22 ⇒ 16 + (x − 2) = 22 ⇒ **x = 8** (consistent with x ≥ 3).

Check: CT = 6, 10, 19, 22 → WT = 1, 6, 9, 6 → 22 / 4 = 5.5 ✓.
questions.trap: Forgetting the switch before the first dispatch or before P4, or ignoring that P4 waits only if P3 is still running at 14 (the idle regime x ≤ 3).

questions.stem:
Three processes each perform CPU → I/O → CPU:

| Process | Arrival | CPU | I/O | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| P2 | 1 | 2 | 5 | 1 |
| P3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 2 |

The CPU is scheduled FCFS (a process returning from I/O joins the tail of the ready queue). There is a **single** I/O device, served FCFS: a process that finishes its CPU burst while the device is busy waits for it. Ignore context-switch time. The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Track both resources.

- P1: CPU 0–4, I/O 4–7, ready at 7.
- P2: CPU 4–6; device busy with P1 until 7 → I/O 7–12, ready at 12.
- P3: CPU 6–9; device busy until 12 → I/O 12–14, ready at 14.
- CPU: P1 is ready at 7 but the CPU is busy with P3 until 9 → P1 9–11 (done). Idle 11–12. P2 12–13 (done). Idle 13–14. P3 14–16 (done).

CPU Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 | idle | P2 | idle | P3 |
0    4    6    9    11     12   13     14   16
```
I/O device:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 |
4    7    12   14
```

TAT: P1 = 11, P2 = 13 − 1 = 12, P3 = 16 − 2 = 14. Average = 37 / 3 = **12.33**.
questions.trap: Letting the I/O operations overlap (each process with its own device) gives P2 back at 11 and P3 at 11, and an average of 11.33.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about FCFS scheduling are TRUE? (Ignore context-switch time.)
options: If all processes arrive at time 0 in non-decreasing order of burst length, FCFS produces the same schedule as non-preemptive SJF.
Round Robin with a time quantum at least as large as the longest CPU burst produces the same schedule as FCFS.
FCFS is well suited to time-sharing systems because each user gets the CPU at regular intervals.
Under FCFS, the waiting time of a process depends only on the bursts of processes ahead of it in the queue (and the arrival times), not on those behind it.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: SJF would pick exactly this order.
- **B** True: no burst is ever cut by the quantum, so each process runs to completion in queue order.
- **C** False: a long burst can hold the CPU for an arbitrarily long time; time-sharing needs preemption (RR).
- **D** True: FCFS never lets a later arrival overtake; a process's start time is determined by the processes ahead of it.
option_feedback: True.
True — RR degenerates to FCFS for a large quantum.
False — FCFS gives no bound on response time.
True — later processes cannot affect an earlier one under FCFS.

questions.stem:
Four processes are in the ready queue at time 0, in the order P1, P2, P3, P4, with CPU bursts 8, x, 3 and 5 respectively (x is a positive integer). Let W_F be the average waiting time under FCFS (queue order) and W_S the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF (ties by queue order). Ignore context-switch time.

If W_F − W_S = 3.75, the **sum of all possible values** of x is ______.
questions.explanation:
With all jobs present at 0, the total waiting time of a sequence (a, b, c, d) is 3a + 2b + c.

FCFS (8, x, 3, 5): total = 24 + 2x + 3 = 27 + 2x.

SJF total depends on where x falls among 3, 5, 8:

| Range | SJF order | SJF total | Difference (total) |
|---|---|---|---|
| x ≤ 3 | x, 3, 5, 8 | 3x + 6 + 5 = 3x + 11 | 16 − x |
| 3 ≤ x ≤ 5 | 3, x, 5, 8 | 9 + 2x + 5 = 2x + 14 | 13 |
| 5 ≤ x ≤ 8 | 3, 5, x, 8 | 9 + 10 + x = x + 19 | x + 8 |
| x ≥ 8 | 3, 5, 8, x | 27 | 2x |

W_F − W_S = 3.75 ⇔ total difference = 15:
- x ≤ 3: 16 − x = 15 → **x = 1** ✓
- 3 ≤ x ≤ 5: 13 ≠ 15
- 5 ≤ x ≤ 8: x + 8 = 15 → **x = 7** ✓
- x ≥ 8: 2x = 15 → not an integer

Sum = 1 + 7 = **8**.

The difference is V-shaped in x: it falls while x is the smallest job (moving x later in the SJF order costs less), is flat while x sits second, and rises again once x is larger than 5.
questions.trap: Assuming the difference grows monotonically with x and reporting only x = 7, or forgetting that the last job's burst never contributes to waiting time.

questions.stem: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) scheduling is
options: the non-preemptive version of SJF
priority scheduling in which priority = arrival time
Round Robin with a quantum equal to the shortest burst
the preemptive version of SJF
questions.explanation: SRTF is preemptive SJF: whenever a new process arrives whose CPU burst is shorter than the *remaining* time of the running process, the running process is preempted.
option_feedback: Non-preemptive SJF lets the running job finish.
Priority = arrival time gives FCFS.
RR ignores burst lengths.
Correct.

questions.stem: The main practical difficulty in implementing SJF for short-term CPU scheduling is that
options: it causes the convoy effect
it needs a very small time quantum
the length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance
it can only be implemented on multiprocessors
questions.explanation: SJF needs the length of each process's *next* CPU burst, which the OS cannot know. It is therefore approximated by predicting the next burst from past bursts, typically by exponential averaging τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ.
option_feedback: Convoy effect is an FCFS problem.
SJF has no quantum.
Correct.
SJF has nothing to do with multiprocessors.

questions.stem: Next CPU bursts are predicted by τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ, where tₙ is the measured length of the n-th burst. Which statement is correct?
options: With α = 0 the prediction equals the most recent actual burst.
With α = 1 recent history has no effect on the prediction.
With α = 1 the prediction equals the most recent actual burst; with α = 0 it never changes from τ₀.
With α = 0.5 only the two most recent bursts influence the prediction.
questions.explanation: α = 1 → τₙ₊₁ = tₙ (only the last burst matters). α = 0 → τₙ₊₁ = τₙ = … = τ₀ (measurements ignored). For 0 < α < 1, expanding gives τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·α·tₙ₋₁ + … + (1 − α)ⁿ⁺¹·τ₀, so *every* past burst contributes, with exponentially decreasing weight.
option_feedback: α = 0 ignores measurements altogether.
Reversed: α = 0 is the case where recent history has no effect.
Correct.
All past bursts contribute, with weights α, α(1 − α), α(1 − α)², …

questions.stem: Using τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ with α = 0.5, the predicted length of a process's last CPU burst was 10 ms and the burst actually took 6 ms. The predicted length (in ms) of its next burst is ______.

A process's CPU bursts are predicted with τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ, α = 0.5 and initial guess τ₀ = 10 ms. Its first four bursts measure t₀ = 6, t₁ = 4, t₂ = 6, t₃ = 4 ms. The predicted length (in ms) of the fifth burst, τ₄, is ______.
questions.trap: Off-by-one: stopping at τ₃ = 6 (the prediction for the fourth burst).

questions.stem:
Using **non-preemptive SJF** (ties in burst length broken by earlier arrival; ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 7 |
| P2 | 2 | 4 |
| P3 | 4 | 1 |
| P4 | 5 | 4 |
| P5 | 6 | 2 |

The average waiting time is ______ (correct to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
At 0 only P1 is present, so it runs to completion (non-preemptive). At 7 all others are waiting: P3 (1), P5 (2), then P2 and P4 (both 4; P2 arrived earlier).

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P3 | P5 | P2 | P4 |
0    7    8    10   14   18
```

| Process | AT | BT | CT | TAT = CT − AT | WT = TAT − BT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 7 | 7 | 7 | 0 |
| P2 | 2 | 4 | 14 | 12 | 8 |
| P3 | 4 | 1 | 8 | 4 | 3 |
| P4 | 5 | 4 | 18 | 13 | 9 |
| P5 | 6 | 2 | 10 | 4 | 2 |

Average WT = (0 + 8 + 3 + 9 + 2) / 5 = 22 / 5 = **4.4**.
questions.trap: Preempting P1 when P3 arrives — that would be SRTF, not non-preemptive SJF.

questions.stem:
Using **SRTF** (preemptive SJF; ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 7 |
| P2 | 1 | 5 |
| P3 | 2 | 9 |
| P4 | 3 | 2 |
| P5 | 5 | 1 |

The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to one decimal place).

A non-preemptive SJF scheduler orders processes by their **predicted** next CPU burst τ = α·t + (1 − α)·τ_prev with α = 0.5, where t is the length of the previous burst and τ_prev the prediction that was made for it. The actual bursts then run for their true lengths. Ties in prediction go to the earlier arrival; ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Previous prediction τ_prev | Previous actual burst t | Actual next burst |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 10 | 6 | 5 |
| P2 | 1 | 4 | 8 | 7 |
| P3 | 2 | 12 | 2 | 3 |
| P4 | 3 | 6 | 2 | 6 |

The average waiting time (using actual bursts) is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
**Predictions** (0.5·t + 0.5·τ_prev): P1 = 3 + 5 = 8, P2 = 4 + 2 = 6, P3 = 1 + 6 = 7, P4 = 1 + 3 = 4.

**Schedule** (decisions by prediction, durations by actual burst):
- 0: only P1 → runs its actual 5 units, 0–5.
- 5: P2 (6), P3 (7), P4 (4) waiting → P4 (smallest prediction) 5–11.
- 11: P2 (6) before P3 (7) → P2 11–18, then P3 18–21.
```
| P1 | P4 | P2 | P3 |
0    5    11   18   21
```

| Process | AT | Actual BT | CT | WT = CT − AT − BT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| P2 | 1 | 7 | 18 | 10 |
| P3 | 2 | 3 | 21 | 16 |
| P4 | 3 | 6 | 11 | 2 |

Average WT = 28 / 4 = **7.00**.

With perfect knowledge (SJF on actual bursts: P3, P4, P2 after P1) the average would be 5.25 — the poor prediction for P3 costs 1.75 units on average.
questions.trap: Ordering by the actual bursts (gives 5.25), or using the predicted lengths as the run times.

questions.stem: CPU bursts are predicted with τₙ₊₁ = α·tₙ + (1 − α)·τₙ, where 0 < α < 1. The initial guess is τ₀ = 12 ms; the first two measured bursts are t₀ = 8 ms and t₁ = 4 ms; the resulting prediction for the third burst is τ₂ = 7 ms. The value of α is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.trap: Using t₁ to compute τ₁ (shifting the indices by one).

questions.stem: Consider SRTF on a single CPU with zero context-switch time, where a running process is preempted only by a newcomer with **strictly** smaller remaining time. Which statements are TRUE?
options: Preemptions can happen only at instants when some process arrives (or returns from I/O).
With n process arrivals in total, the number of preemptions is at most n − 1.
SRTF never starves a process, because every process's remaining time eventually becomes the smallest.
If every process arrives at time 0, SRTF performs no preemption at all.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: between arrivals the running process's remaining time only decreases while others' stay fixed, so it stays the minimum.
- **B** True: each arrival causes at most one preemption, and the first arrival (into an idle CPU) causes none, so ≤ n − 1.
- **C** False: a long process can be bypassed forever by a steady stream of short arrivals — its remaining time does not shrink while it waits.
- **D** True: with no later arrivals there is nothing to preempt the shortest job, which simply runs to completion each time.
option_feedback: True.
True — at most one preemption per arrival, none for the first.
False — waiting does not reduce remaining time, so starvation is possible.
True — SRTF degenerates to SJF.

questions.stem: Consider single-CPU scheduling of processes that each have one CPU burst and no I/O, with zero context-switch time. Under SRTF a running process is preempted only by a strictly smaller remaining time, and ties among ready processes go to the earlier arrival, then the lower index. Non-preemptive SJF uses the same tie rule. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: For some input, a process has a strictly larger turnaround time under SRTF than under FCFS.
For every input, the maximum turnaround time (over all processes) under SRTF is at most that under non-preemptive SJF.
For every input, each process's response time (first dispatch − arrival) under SRTF is at most its response time under non-preemptive SJF.
For every input, the average turnaround time under SRTF is at most that under non-preemptive SJF.
questions.explanation:
- **A True.** P1 (AT 0, BT 10), P2 (AT 1, BT 1). FCFS: P1 completes at 10 (TAT 10). SRTF: P2 preempts at 1, P1 completes at 11 (TAT 11).
- **B False.** P1 (0, 10), P2 (1, 2), P3 (3, 2).
  - SJF: P1 0–10, P2 10–12, P3 12–14 → TATs 10, 11, 11 → max 11.
  - SRTF: P1 0–1, P2 1–3, P3 3–5, P1 5–14 → P1's TAT = 14 → max 14.
  SRTF optimises the *average*, and it does so by pushing the long job back further.
- **C False.** P1 (0, 4), P2 (1, 2), P3 (1, 2), P4 (4, 1).
  - SRTF: at 1, P2 (2) < P1's 3 → P2 1–3; P3 (2) < P1's 3 → P3 3–5. At 4, P4 (1) arrives but P3 also has 1 left — no strict improvement, so P4 waits; P4 runs 5–6 → response time **1**.
  - SJF: P1 runs 0–4 uninterrupted; at 4 the shortest waiting job is P4 → P4 4–5 → response time **0**.
  Preemption helped P2 and P3 jump ahead, and they then blocked P4.
- **D True.** SRTF minimises average waiting (and so average turnaround) time over *all* schedules of single-burst processes, including the non-preemptive SJF schedule.
option_feedback: True: a long job preempted by a later short one finishes later than under FCFS (e.g. P1 (0, 10), P2 (1, 1): 11 vs 10).
False: P1 (0, 10), P2 (1, 2), P3 (3, 2) gives max TAT 14 under SRTF but 11 under SJF — SRTF optimises the average, not the maximum.
False: P1 (0, 4), P2 (1, 2), P3 (1, 2), P4 (4, 1): P4's response time is 1 under SRTF but 0 under SJF.
True: SRTF is optimal for average waiting/turnaround time among all schedules, so it can never be worse than SJF on average.
questions.trap: Generalising SRTF's optimality of the *average* to per-process or worst-case guarantees (B and C).

questions.stem:
Four processes are scheduled once by **SRTF** and once by **non-preemptive SJF**. In both, a running process is never preempted on an equal remaining time and ties among ready processes go to the earlier arrival. Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 9 |
| P2 | 2 | x |
| P3 | 4 | 3 |
| P4 | 5 | 6 |

x is a positive integer. For how many values of x with 1 ≤ x ≤ 20 is the average waiting time under SJF **at least 1.25 more** than under SRTF?
questions.explanation:
Work with total waiting time; the condition is W_SJF − W_SRTF ≥ 4 × 1.25 = 5.

**Non-preemptive SJF.** P1 runs 0–9; at 9 all others wait and run in order of burst.
- x ≤ 3 (P2 wins a tie at 3 by earlier arrival): P2, P3, P4 → WT 7, 5 + x, 7 + x → 19 + 2x.
- 3 < x ≤ 6: P3, P2, P4 → WT 5, 10, 7 + x → 22 + x.
- x > 6: P3, P4, P2 → WT 5, 7, 16 → 28.

**SRTF.** At 2, P1 has 7 left, so P2 preempts iff x < 7.
- x = 1: P2 2–3; P1 3–4; P3 preempts (P1 has 6 left) 4–7; at 7 P1 (6) ties P4 (6) → P1 (earlier) 7–13, P4 13–19 → WT 4, 0, 0, 8 = **12**.
- x = 2: P2 2–4; P3 4–7; P4 (6) < P1 (7) → P4 7–13, P1 13–20 → WT 11, 0, 0, 2 = **13**.
- 3 ≤ x ≤ 5: at 4 P2 has x − 2 ≤ 3 left → no preemption by P3. P2 2 → 2 + x, P3 → 5 + x, P4 → 11 + x, P1 → 18 + x → WT (9 + x) + 0 + (x − 2) + x = **3x + 7**.
- x = 6: at 4 P2 has 4 left > 3 → P3 preempts 4–7; P2 7–11, P4 11–17, P1 17–24 → WT 15, 3, 0, 6 = **24**.
- x ≥ 7: no preemption at 2. P1 0–4, P3 preempts 4–7, P1 (5 left) 7–12, P4 12–18, P2 18 → WT 3, 16, 0, 7 = **26**.

| x | W_SJF | W_SRTF | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 21 | 12 | 9 |
| 2 | 23 | 13 | 10 |
| 3 | 25 | 16 | 9 |
| 4 | 26 | 19 | 7 |
| 5 | 27 | 22 | 5 |
| 6 | 28 | 24 | 4 |
| ≥ 7 | 28 | 26 | 2 |

Difference ≥ 5 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → **5** values.
questions.trap: Missing the regime changes (P3 preempts P2 only when x = 6; P2 does not preempt P1 at all once x ≥ 7) or the tie between P1 and P4 at t = 7 when x = 1; treating x = 5 (difference exactly 1.25) as failing.

questions.stem: Processes P1 (arrival 0, burst 10) and P2 (arrival 1, burst 2) are scheduled. Under SRTF, when does P2 complete, and under non-preemptive SJF when does P2 complete?
options: 3 under SRTF and 12 under SJF
12 under both
3 under both
2 under SRTF and 12 under SJF
questions.explanation:
SRTF: at 1, P1 has 9 left > 2 → P2 runs 1–3, completes at **3**.
```
| P1 | P2 |    P1    |
0    1    3          12
```
Non-preemptive SJF: P1 started at 0 and cannot be interrupted → P2 runs 10–12, completes at **12**.
```
|    P1    | P2 |
0          10   12
```
option_feedback: Correct.
SRTF would preempt P1 at time 1.
Non-preemptive SJF cannot interrupt P1.
P2 arrives at 1, so it cannot finish before 3.

questions.stem: In priority scheduling, the technique of gradually increasing the priority of processes that have waited in the system for a long time is called
options: aging
thrashing
swapping
priority inversion
questions.explanation: **Aging** raises the priority of long-waiting processes so that a low-priority process eventually becomes the highest-priority one and runs — it is the standard cure for starvation (indefinite blocking) in priority scheduling.
option_feedback: Correct.
Thrashing is excessive paging.
Swapping moves whole processes between memory and disk.
Priority inversion is a high-priority process waiting on a lock held by a low-priority one.

questions.stem: In Highest Response Ratio Next (HRRN) scheduling, with W = time spent waiting so far and S = expected service (burst) time, the response ratio of a process is
options: W / S
S / (W + S)
(W + S) / S
(W + S) / W
questions.explanation: Response ratio R = (W + S) / S = 1 + W/S. It starts at 1 and grows while the process waits — faster for short jobs (favouring them like SJF) but without bound for long jobs too (so they cannot starve). HRRN is non-preemptive and picks the largest R whenever the CPU becomes free.
option_feedback: Missing the +1; it is 1 + W/S.
This is the reciprocal; it would favour long-waiting processes less.
Correct.
The denominator is the service time, not the waiting time.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correctly described as a special case of priority scheduling (smaller value = higher priority)?
options: Round Robin, with priority = time quantum
SRTF, with priority = arrival time
FCFS, with priority = burst length
SJF, with priority = (predicted) next CPU burst length
questions.explanation: SJF is priority scheduling where the priority is the predicted next CPU burst — the shorter the burst, the higher the priority. (FCFS would be priority = arrival time; SRTF would be preemptive priority = remaining time. RR is not a priority scheme.)
option_feedback: RR does not prioritise processes.
Priority = arrival time gives FCFS behaviour, not SRTF.
Priority = burst length gives SJF, not FCFS.
Correct.

questions.stem: Under HRRN scheduling, a process with expected service time 5 ms arrived at time 4 ms. If the CPU becomes free at time 19 ms and the process is still waiting, its response ratio at that instant is ______.
questions.trap: Using W / S = 3, or measuring waiting from time 0.

questions.stem:
Using **non-preemptive priority** scheduling (smaller number = higher priority; equal priorities broken by earlier arrival; ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 3 |
| P2 | 1 | 3 | 1 |
| P3 | 2 | 6 | 4 |
| P4 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| P5 | 4 | 4 | 1 |

The average waiting time is ______ (correct to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
P1 runs 0–5 uninterrupted. At 5 everyone is waiting: P2 and P5 have priority 1 (P2 arrived first), then P4 (2), then P3 (4).

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P5 | P4 | P3 |
0    5    8    12   14   20
```

| Process | AT | BT | CT | TAT = CT − AT | WT = TAT − BT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 0 |
| P2 | 1 | 3 | 8 | 7 | 4 |
| P3 | 2 | 6 | 20 | 18 | 12 |
| P4 | 3 | 2 | 14 | 11 | 9 |
| P5 | 4 | 4 | 12 | 8 | 4 |

Average WT = (0 + 4 + 12 + 9 + 4) / 5 = 29 / 5 = **5.8**.
questions.trap: Preempting P1 at time 1 (that is the preemptive variant).

questions.stem:
Using **preemptive priority** scheduling where a **larger number means higher priority** (ignore context-switch time):

| Process | Arrival | Burst | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 2 |
| P2 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
| P3 | 3 | 2 | 5 |
| P4 | 4 | 6 | 1 |
| P5 | 6 | 3 | 4 |

The completion time of **P2** is ______.
questions.explanation:
- 0: P1 (2) runs. 1: P2 (3) > 2 → preempts.
- 3: P3 (5) preempts P2 (P2 has 2 left). P3 runs 3–5.
- 4: P4 (1) arrives — lowest, waits.
- 5: highest ready is P2 (3) → runs 5–6.
- 6: P5 (4) preempts P2 (1 left). P5 runs 6–9.
- 9: P2 (3) runs 9–10 → **done at 10**. Then P1 10–14, P4 14–20.

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P2 | P5 | P2 | P1 | P4 |
0    1    3    5    6    9    10   14   20
```
questions.trap: Treating the smaller number as higher priority (the usual textbook convention) — read the convention in the stem.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next) scheduling are TRUE?
options: It is non-preemptive.
Among processes that have waited equally long, it prefers the one with the shorter service time.
A long process can starve if short processes keep arriving.
Among processes with equal service time, it prefers the one that has waited longer.
questions.explanation:
R = 1 + W/S.
- **A** True: the ratio is evaluated only when the CPU becomes free.
- **B** True: same W, smaller S → larger W/S.
- **C** False: a waiting process's W grows without bound, so its ratio eventually exceeds that of any newcomer (whose ratio starts at 1). HRRN has built-in aging.
- **D** True: same S, larger W → larger ratio.
option_feedback: True.
True — it favours short jobs like SJF.
False — the growing W/S term prevents starvation.
True — it favours old jobs like FCFS.

questions.stem:
Processes are scheduled by **preemptive priority** (smaller number = higher priority). Processes of **equal** priority share the CPU by Round Robin with quantum 2. A process preempted by a higher-priority arrival goes to the tail of its own priority's RR queue and gets a fresh quantum next time; a process arriving at a quantum boundary is queued before the process whose quantum just expired. Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 2 |
| P2 | 0 | 3 | 3 |
| P3 | 1 | 4 | 2 |
| P4 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
| P5 | 7 | 3 | 2 |

The average waiting time is ______ (correct to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Priority-2 RR queue shown in brackets.
- 0–2 P1 (priority 2; P2 has priority 3). P3 arrives at 1 → [P3]. At 2 P1's quantum ends → [P3, P1].
- 2–4 P3. At 4 P4 (priority 1) arrives and P3's quantum ends → [P1, P3]; P4 runs 4–6 (done).
- 6–8 P1 (1 left). P5 arrives at 7 → [P3, P5]; at 8 → [P3, P5, P1].
- 8–10 P3 (done). 10–12 P5 (1 left) → [P1, P5]. 12–13 P1 (done). 13–14 P5 (done).
- 14–17 P2 (only priority-3 process).

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P3 | P4 | P1 | P3 | P5 | P1 | P5 | P2 |
0    2    4    6    8    10   12   13   14   17
```

| Process | AT | BT | CT | WT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 5 | 13 | 8 |
| P2 | 0 | 3 | 17 | 14 |
| P3 | 1 | 4 | 10 | 5 |
| P4 | 4 | 2 | 6 | 0 |
| P5 | 7 | 3 | 14 | 4 |

Average WT = 31 / 5 = **6.2**.
questions.trap: Running equal-priority processes FCFS (P1 0–4 first) gives 5.8; letting P2 run before the priority-2 work is finished ignores priority.

questions.stem:
Four processes are to be scheduled by **preemptive priority** with **static** priorities. You may assign the priorities 1, 2, 3, 4 to the processes in any one-to-one way (1 = highest). Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 4 |
| P2 | 2 | 8 |
| P3 | 6 | 1 |
| P4 | 8 | 6 |

Over all 4! assignments, the minimum possible average waiting time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
**Lower bound.** SRTF minimises average waiting time over *every* schedule, so no priority assignment can beat it.

SRTF: P1 0–4 (P2's 8 never beats P1's remaining time); P2 4–6; P3 (1) preempts P2 (6 left) 6–7; P2 7–13 — at 8 P4 (6) does not beat P2's 5; P4 13–19.
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P2 | P4 |
0    4    6    7    13   19
```
WT = 0 + 3 + 0 + 5 = 8 → average 2.00.

**Achieving it with static priorities.** We need P1 above P2 (no preemption at 2), P3 above P2 (preempt at 6) and P2 above P4 (no preemption at 8). E.g. P3 = 1, P1 = 2, P2 = 3, P4 = 4 reproduces exactly the SRTF chart, so the minimum is 8 / 4 = **2.00**.

**The natural guess fails.** 'Shortest burst = highest priority' (P3 = 1, P1 = 2, P4 = 3, P2 = 4) lets P4 preempt P2 at 8 even though P2 then has only 5 left:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P2 | P4 | P2 |
0    4    6    7    8    14   19
```
WT = 0 + 9 + 0 + 0 = 9 → 2.25.
questions.trap: Ranking priorities by total burst length (2.25): what matters is the remaining time at each decision point, so the long job P2 must outrank P4.

questions.stem:
Four processes are scheduled by **HRRN** (non-preemptive; response ratio = (waiting time + service time) / service time; ties go to the earlier arrival). Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Service time |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 5 |
| B | 1 | 6 |
| C | 2 | 3 |
| D | a | 4 |

a is a positive integer. The **largest** value of a for which D completes before B is ______.
questions.explanation:
A runs 0–5 regardless of a.

**Decision at t = 5** (if D has arrived): C = (3 + 3)/3 = 2, B = (4 + 6)/6 ≈ 1.67, D = (5 − a + 4)/4 = (9 − a)/4. D beats C only if (9 − a)/4 > 2, i.e. a < 1 (a = 1 ties and D wins by earlier arrival — either way D will finish before B). For a ≥ 2, **C** runs 5–8.

**Decision at t = 8** (between B and D): B = (7 + 6)/6 = 13/6 ≈ 2.17, D = (8 − a + 4)/4 = (12 − a)/4.
D wins ⇔ (12 − a)/4 > 13/6 ⇔ 12 − a > 8.67 ⇔ a < 3.33 ⇔ **a ≤ 3**.

- a = 3: D = 9/4 = 2.25 > 2.17 → D 8–12, B 12–18 ✓.
- a = 4: D = 2.0 < 2.17 → B 8–14, D 14–18 ✗. Larger a only lowers D's ratio (and for a > 8 D is not even present).

Largest a = **3**.
questions.trap: Picking D at 8 because it is shorter than B (that is SJF), or measuring D's waiting time from 0 instead of from a.

questions.stem: A preemptive priority scheduler uses **dynamic** priorities: every process has priority 0 when it enters the ready queue; while it waits in the ready queue its priority changes at rate α per unit time, and while it runs its priority changes at rate β per unit time. A **larger** value means higher priority; the running process is preempted only when some ready process has a **strictly** higher priority; ties go to the earlier arrival. Processes have a single CPU burst. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: If β > α > 0, the scheduler behaves exactly like FCFS.
If α < β < 0, the scheduler behaves like preemptive LIFO (the most recently arrived process runs).
If α > β > 0, the scheduler behaves exactly like FCFS.
If α > 0 > β, a newly arrived process can never preempt the running process.
questions.explanation:
- **A True.** A newcomer starts at 0, below every process already present (all of them have positive priority). Waiting processes all rise at the same rate α, so the earliest arrival is always highest among them. The running process was the highest when dispatched and rises *faster* (β > α), so nobody ever overtakes it. Result: run to completion in arrival order = FCFS.
- **B True.** Every process that has been in the system for a while has a negative priority, so a newcomer at 0 immediately preempts. Waiting processes fall faster (α < β), so the most recent arrival always has the highest priority among those present → preemptive LIFO.
- **C False.** Now waiting processes rise faster than the running one. A waiting process eventually overtakes the running process and preempts it, which then waits and climbs faster... the CPU ends up being shared in round-robin fashion, not FCFS.
- **D False.** The running process's priority falls at |β|; once it has run long enough to drop below 0, a newcomer (priority 0) preempts it.
option_feedback: True: newcomers start lowest, waiting processes keep arrival order, and the running one climbs fastest, so nobody preempts it.
True: a newcomer at 0 beats everyone already in the system (all negative), and later arrivals have fallen least.
False: waiting processes climb faster than the running one, so they overtake it — RR-like time sharing, not FCFS.
False: the running priority drops below 0 after a while, and a newcomer at 0 then preempts it.
questions.trap: Assuming 'priority grows while waiting' always means FCFS; the behaviour depends on how α compares with β.

questions.stem: Consider a generic priority scheduler on one CPU (smaller value = higher priority; ties go to the earlier arrival; zero switch cost). Which statements are TRUE?
options: Preemptive priority with priority = remaining CPU time behaves exactly like SRTF.
Non-preemptive priority with priority = arrival time behaves exactly like FCFS.
With static priorities and no aging, the lowest-priority process is guaranteed to complete once all higher-priority processes present at its arrival have completed.
Preemptive priority with priority value = (current time − arrival time), re-evaluated continuously, behaves exactly like FCFS.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: that is the definition of SRTF.
- **B** True: the earliest arrival always has the smallest value.
- **C** False: higher-priority processes that arrive *later* can keep overtaking it — that is exactly starvation.
- **D** False: the value (now − arrival) is largest for the oldest process, i.e. it has the *lowest* priority; a new arrival (value 0) always wins and preempts. It behaves like preemptive LIFO, not FCFS.
option_feedback: True.
True.
False — later high-priority arrivals can postpone it indefinitely.
False — 'now − arrival' is largest for the oldest process, which therefore has the lowest priority; the scheme is LIFO-like.
questions.trap: Reading 'waited longest' as 'highest priority' without checking which direction the numeric value moves.

questions.stem: If the time quantum of Round Robin scheduling is made larger than the longest CPU burst of any process, RR behaves like
options: SJF
SRTF
FCFS
Priority scheduling
questions.explanation: No process is ever preempted by quantum expiry, so each runs its whole burst in ready-queue (arrival) order — exactly FCFS.
option_feedback: RR never looks at burst lengths.
RR never looks at remaining times.
Correct.
RR has no notion of priority.

questions.stem: What is the main drawback of making the Round Robin time quantum very small compared with the context-switch time?
options: Processes may starve
The CPU spends a large fraction of its time context switching, lowering useful utilisation
Response time becomes very large
The scheduler degenerates into FCFS
questions.explanation: With quantum q and switch time s, at most q / (q + s) of CPU time is useful. As q shrinks toward s, overhead dominates. (Response time actually *improves* with small q; a *large* q degenerates to FCFS; RR never starves.) A common rule of thumb is that about 80 % of CPU bursts should be shorter than q.
option_feedback: RR is starvation-free.
Correct.
Small q makes response time small, not large.
That happens for a very large quantum.

questions.stem: P1, P2, P3 arrive at time 0 (in that queue order) with CPU bursts 5, 3 and 4 ms. Under Round Robin with a 2 ms quantum (ignore switch time), P2 completes at time ______ ms.
questions.explanation:
Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 |
0    2    4    6    8    9    11   12
```

P2 runs 2–4 (1 ms left) and 8–9 → completes at **9 ms**.

questions.stem: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3 with CPU bursts 7, 4 and 9 ms. Round Robin with quantum 3 ms is used; ignore context-switch time. The average waiting time (in ms) is ______.

Round Robin with quantum 2 (ignore switch time). If a new process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the **new process is enqueued before the preempted one**.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 4 |
| P2 | 2 | 5 |
| P3 | 3 | 2 |

- 0–2 P1. At 2, P2 arrives and P1 expires → queue [P2, P1].
- 2–4 P2 (P3 arrives at 3). Queue [P1, P3, P2].
- 4–6 P1 (done; P4 arrives at 5). Queue [P3, P2, P4].

0    2    4    6    8    10   12   13   14

If a new process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the **new process is enqueued before the preempted one**.

| P2 | 1 | 3 |

The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).

questions.stem:
Ten processes share a CPU under Round Robin with quantum q ms (q an integer, q ≥ 2); every context switch takes 1 ms and one switch precedes every dispatch. Four processes are CPU-bound (they always use the full quantum). Six are I/O-bound: each uses exactly 2 ms of CPU and then blocks, and is back in the ready queue before its next turn. Hence all ten are always in the RR cycle.

Two requirements:
1. After a CPU-bound process's quantum ends, it must get the CPU again within **60 ms** (end of its quantum to the start of its next quantum).
2. CPU utilisation (useful work / total time) must be **at least 80 %**.

The number of integer values of q that satisfy both requirements is ______.
questions.explanation:
**One RR cycle** contains 10 dispatches, so 10 switches: useful time = 4q (CPU-bound) + 6 × 2 (I/O-bound) = 4q + 12; total = 4q + 12 + 10 = 4q + 22.

**Requirement 1.** Between the end of process A's quantum and its next start, the other 9 processes run once — 3 CPU-bound (q each) and 6 I/O-bound (2 each) — with a switch before each of them and one more switch back to A: gap = 3q + 12 + 10 = 3q + 22 ≤ 60 ⇒ q ≤ 12.67 ⇒ q ≤ 12.

**Requirement 2.** (4q + 12) / (4q + 22) ≥ 0.8 ⇒ 4q + 12 ≥ 3.2q + 17.6 ⇒ 0.8q ≥ 5.6 ⇒ q ≥ 7.

q ∈ {7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12} → **6** values.
questions.trap: Charging the I/O-bound processes a full quantum (gives 9q + 10 ≤ 60 and an empty range), counting A's own quantum in the gap, or using 9 switches instead of 10.

questions.stem:
Round Robin with quantum 2 (ignore switch time). If a new process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the **new process is enqueued before the preempted one**; processes arriving at the same instant are queued in index order.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 3 |
| P2 | 1 | 6 |
| P3 | 2 | 4 |
| P4 | a | 2 |

a is a non-negative integer. The **largest** value of a for which P4 completes before P2 is ______.
questions.explanation:
P2 needs three quanta (6 = 2 + 2 + 2); P4 needs one. So P4 finishes before P2 iff P4 is queued ahead of P2 when P2 rejoins the queue for its **third** quantum.

Schedule without P4 interfering (P4 arriving late):
- 0–2 P1. At 2: P3 arrives (queued before the preempted P1) → [P2, P3, P1].
- 2–4 P2 → [P3, P1, P2]. 4–6 P3 → [P1, P2, P3]. 6–7 P1 (done).
- 7–9 P2 (second quantum) → at **9** P2 rejoins the queue → [P3, P2]. 9–11 P3 (done), 11–13 P2 (done).

If P4 arrives at a ≤ 8, it is already in the queue at 9, ahead of P2, and finishes in one quantum before P2's last turn. (An earlier P4 only delays the instant at which P2 rejoins, so the conclusion still holds.)

**a = 9:** P4 arrives exactly as P2's quantum expires → by the convention P4 is queued **before** P2: [P3, P4, P2] → P3 9–11, P4 11–13, P2 13–15. P4 (13) completes before P2 (15) ✓.

**a = 10:** queue is already [P3, P2] → P2 11–13 finishes before P4 (13–15) ✗.

Largest a = **9**.
questions.trap: Applying the opposite convention at the boundary (answer 8), or thinking P4 must arrive before P2's second quantum starts (answer 7).

questions.stem: Consider Round Robin with quantum q and zero context-switch time. Which statements are TRUE?
options: If q is at least the longest CPU burst, RR produces the same schedule as FCFS.
If there are n processes in total (including the preempted one) and no new processes arrive, a preempted process waits at most (n − 1)·q before it runs again.
For processes all arriving at time 0, RR never gives a smaller average waiting time than FCFS in the same queue order.
If all n processes arrive at time 0 and every burst is at least q, the k-th process in the queue first gets the CPU at time (k − 1)·q.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: no burst is ever cut.
- **B** True: at most the other n − 1 processes each run ≤ q before its next turn.
- **C** False: queue order P1 (10), P2 (1). FCFS: WT = 0, 10 → avg 5. RR q = 1: P1 0–1, P2 1–2, P1 2–11 → WT = 1, 1 → avg 1.
- **D** True: each earlier process runs exactly q in the first round.
option_feedback: True.
True — the standard RR waiting bound.
False — RR helps short jobs stuck behind a long one.
True.

questions.stem:
Four processes P1, P2, P3, P4 are in the ready queue at time 0 in that order. Their CPU bursts b1, b2, b3, b4 are unknown positive integers. They are scheduled by Round Robin with quantum 3. Every dispatch (including the first one at time 0) is preceded by a 1-unit context switch; no switch is needed if a process simply continues because no other process is ready. The observed completion times are:

| Process | P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Completion time | 28 | 7 | 30 | 25 |

The value of b3 is ______.
questions.explanation:
Rebuild the chart round by round. A process completes in a slice of length < 3 or exactly 3; it is still alive if its completion time is later.

**Round 1**
- CS 0–1, P1 1–4: P1 completes at 28, so it is not done → b1 > 3.
- CS 4–5, P2 starts at 5 and completes at 7 → slice of 2 → **b2 = 2**.
- CS 7–8, P3 8–11 (not done, b3 > 3). CS 11–12, P4 12–15 (not done, b4 > 3).

**Round 2** (queue P1, P3, P4)
- CS 15–16, P1 16–19 (completes at 28 > 19 → b1 > 6).
- CS 19–20, P3 20–23 (completes at 30 → b3 > 6).
- CS 23–24, P4 starts at 24 and completes at 25 → slice 1 → b4 = 3 + 1 = 4.

**Round 3** (queue P1, P3)
- CS 25–26, P1 26–28 → slice 2 → b1 = 3 + 3 + 2 = 8.
- CS 28–29, P3 29–30 → slice 1 → **b3 = 3 + 3 + 1 = 7**.

Check: the chart has 9 dispatches → 9 switches, and 30 = 9 + (8 + 2 + 7 + 4) ✓.
```
|CS|P1|CS|P2|CS|P3|CS|P4|CS|P1|CS|P3|CS|P4|CS|P1|CS|P3|
0  1  4  5  7  8  11 12 15 16 19 20 23 24 25 26 28 29 30
```
questions.trap: Ignoring the switches and reading b3 off the completion times directly (e.g. treating 30 as the sum of bursts), or forgetting that the switch before P2 means P2 starts at 5, not 4.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a multilevel queue (MLQ) and a multilevel **feedback** queue (MLFQ) scheduler?
options: MLQ uses several ready queues; MLFQ uses a single ready queue
MLFQ uses FCFS in every queue; MLQ uses RR in every queue
MLQ is always preemptive; MLFQ is always non-preemptive
In MLQ a process is permanently assigned to one queue; in MLFQ a process can move between queues
questions.explanation: In MLQ, processes are classified once (e.g. system, interactive, batch) and stay in that queue. MLFQ lets processes move: typically a process that uses its full quantum is demoted, and a process that waits too long may be promoted (aging). Both use several queues, each with its own algorithm.
option_feedback: Both use multiple queues.
Each queue can use any algorithm in both schemes.
Either can be preemptive between queues.
Correct.

questions.stem: A multilevel queue scheduler has a foreground (interactive) queue with absolute priority over a background (batch) queue. Which problem can this cause?
options: Belady's anomaly
Convoy effect in the foreground queue
Starvation of background processes
Deadlock between the two queues
questions.explanation: With fixed priority between queues, background processes run only when the foreground queue is empty; a steady stream of interactive work can starve them. Remedies: time-slice between queues (e.g. 80 % / 20 %) or use feedback/aging.
option_feedback: That is a page-replacement phenomenon.
The foreground queue is usually RR, which avoids convoys.
Correct.
Scheduling queues do not hold resources; no deadlock.

questions.stem: Which of the following are parameters that must be specified to define a multilevel feedback queue scheduler?
options: The number of queues and the scheduling algorithm for each queue
The method used to decide when to demote a process to a lower-priority queue
The method used to decide which queue a process enters when it needs service
The page-replacement policy used for each queue
questions.explanation: Silberschatz lists: number of queues, the algorithm for each queue, when to upgrade (promote) a process, when to demote it, and which queue a process enters when it needs service. Page replacement has nothing to do with CPU scheduling queues.
option_feedback: Yes.
Yes.
Yes.
No — memory management, not CPU scheduling.

questions.stem: In a typical MLFQ (new processes enter the top queue with the smallest quantum; a process that uses its whole quantum is demoted), which processes tend to remain in the highest-priority queue?
options: Long CPU-bound processes
I/O-bound and interactive processes with short CPU bursts
Processes that arrived first
Processes with the largest memory footprint
questions.explanation: A process that blocks for I/O before its quantum expires is not demoted, so short-burst (I/O-bound, interactive) processes stay on top and get quick response. CPU-bound processes use full quanta and sink to lower queues. This is how MLFQ approximates SJF without knowing burst lengths.
option_feedback: They are demoted after using full quanta.
Correct.
Arrival order does not keep a process on top.
Memory size is irrelevant to CPU scheduling here.

questions.stem: An MLFQ has three queues: Q0 (RR, quantum 8 ms), Q1 (RR, quantum 16 ms) and Q2 (FCFS). New processes enter Q0, and a process that uses its full quantum is moved down one level. A single process with a 50 ms CPU burst arrives in an otherwise empty system. For how many ms does it execute while in Q2?
questions.explanation: Q0: 8 ms (uses full quantum → demoted). Q1: 16 ms (full → demoted). Remaining = 50 − 8 − 16 = **26 ms**, run in Q2.

questions.stem: An MLFQ has Q0 (RR, quantum 3), Q1 (RR, quantum 6) and Q2 (FCFS). New processes enter Q0; a process that uses its full quantum without finishing moves to the tail of the next lower queue; a lower queue runs only when all higher queues are empty. Processes: A (arrival 0, burst 12), B (arrival 0, burst 5), C (arrival 2, burst 3); A is ahead of B in Q0. Ignore switch time. The completion time of **B** is ______.
questions.explanation:
- Q0: A 0–3 → Q1 (9 left). B 3–6 → Q1 (2 left). C 6–9 (uses exactly 3 and finishes).
- Q1 = [A, B]: A 9–15 (full quantum, 3 left) → Q2. B 15–17 → **done at 17**.
- Q2: A 17–20.

Gantt chart:
```
| A  | B  | C  | A  | B  | A  |
0    3    6    9    15   17   20
```
questions.trap: Letting C (arriving at 2) preempt A in Q0 — both are in the same queue, so C just waits its turn.

questions.stem:
A multilevel queue scheduler has a foreground queue (RR, quantum 2) with absolute, **preemptive** priority over a background queue (FCFS). Processes never change queues. Ignore switch time.

| Process | Queue | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | foreground | 0 | 3 |
| B1 | background | 1 | 6 |
| F2 | foreground | 6 | 4 |
| B2 | background | 9 | 2 |

The completion time of **B1** is ______.
questions.explanation:
- 0–3 F1 (alone in foreground; it continues after its quantum since no one else is in its queue). Done at 3.
- 3–6 B1 (background runs because foreground is empty).
- 6: F2 arrives → preempts B1 (3 left). F2 6–10 (done).
- 10–13 B1 resumes → **done at 13**. B2 (arrived 9, behind B1) 13–15.

Gantt chart:
```
| F1 | B1 | F2 | B1 | B2 |
0    3    6    10   13   15
```

questions.stem: Which statements about multilevel feedback queue scheduling are TRUE?
options: It approximates SJF/SRTF behaviour without needing to know burst lengths in advance.
Without any promotion (aging) mechanism, processes in the lowest queue can starve.
A process's queue is fixed for its lifetime once assigned.
Promoting processes that have waited long in lower queues is a form of aging.
questions.explanation:
- **A** True: short-burst processes finish in high queues; long ones are demoted, so short jobs are favoured.
- **B** True: lower queues run only when higher ones are empty.
- **C** False: that describes plain MLQ; MLFQ moves processes.
- **D** True: promotion after a long wait is exactly aging.
option_feedback: True.
True.
False — that is MLQ.
True.

questions.stem:
An MLFQ has Q0 (RR, quantum 3), Q1 (RR, quantum 6) and Q2 (FCFS). Rules:
- New processes enter the tail of Q0. A process that uses its full quantum without finishing its CPU burst moves to the tail of the next lower queue.
- A process that **blocks for I/O before its quantum expires stays in the same queue**; when its I/O completes it rejoins the tail of that queue with a fresh quantum.
- A process becoming ready in a higher queue immediately preempts a process running from a lower queue; the preempted process goes to the **tail of its own queue** and gets a fresh quantum next time.
- Every process has its own I/O device. Ignore switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | CPU 10 |
| P2 | 1 | CPU 2, I/O 3, CPU 2, I/O 3, CPU 2 |
| P3 | 2 | CPU 7 |

The completion time of **P3** is ______.
questions.explanation:
- 0–3 P1 (Q0, full quantum, 7 left) → Q1.
- 3–5 P2 (Q0): blocks after 2 < 3 → stays in Q0; I/O 5–8.
- 5–8 P3 (Q0, full quantum, 4 left) → Q1 = [P1, P3].
- 8: P2 back in Q0 → 8–10 P2, blocks again; I/O 10–13.
- 10: Q0 empty → P1 from Q1 runs 10–13. At 13 P2 returns to Q0 and preempts; P1 (4 left) goes to the **tail** of Q1 → [P3, P1].
- 13–15 P2 (done).
- 15–19 **P3** from Q1 (4 < 6, finishes) → done at **19**.
- 19–23 P1 (done).

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 | P2 | P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 |
0    3    5    8    10   13   15   19   23
```
questions.trap: Demoting P2 even though it never used a full quantum, or resuming the preempted P1 ahead of P3 (gives 23).

questions.stem:
A multilevel queue scheduler time-slices between its two queues: the **foreground** queue (RR, quantum 2) gets 4 time units, then the **background** queue (FCFS) gets 1 time unit, alternately, starting with the foreground. If one queue is empty, the other gets the CPU. Processes never change queues; ignore switch time. All arrive at time 0:

| Process | Queue | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | foreground | 6 |
| F2 | foreground | 5 |
| B1 | background | 5 |

F1 is ahead of F2 in the foreground queue. The average turnaround time is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Each 4-unit foreground slot holds two RR quanta (F1 then F2).
```
| F1 | F2 | B1 | F1 | F2 | B1 | F1 | F2 | B1  |
0    2    4    5    7    9    10   12   13    16
```
- Slot 1 (0–4): F1 2, F2 2. Background 4–5: B1 (4 left).
- Slot 2 (5–9): F1 2, F2 2. Background 9–10: B1 (3 left).
- Slot 3 (10–14): F1 10–12 (done, 6 total), F2 12–13 (done, 5 total). Foreground is now empty, so B1 gets the CPU 13–16 (done).

TAT: F1 = 12, F2 = 13, B1 = 16. Average = 41 / 3 = **13.67**.
questions.trap: Wasting 13–14 as idle (giving 14.0) — when the foreground empties, the background runs immediately.

questions.stem:
An MLFQ has Q0 (RR, quantum 2), Q1 (RR, quantum 4) and Q2 (FCFS). New processes enter the tail of Q0; a process that uses up its quantum without finishing moves to the tail of the next lower queue. A process arriving in a higher queue immediately preempts a process running from a lower queue. **Here the preempted process is put back at the head of its own queue and keeps the unused part of its current quantum** (it does not get a fresh one). Ignore switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 9 |
| P2 | 1 | 6 |
| P3 | 5 | 3 |

The completion time of **P2** is ______.
questions.explanation:
- 0–2 P1 (Q0, full, 7 left) → Q1.
- 2–4 P2 (Q0, full, 4 left) → Q1 = [P1, P2].
- 4–5 P1 from Q1 (quantum 4, 1 used). At 5 P3 arrives in Q0 → preempts; P1 goes to the **head** of Q1 with 3 units of quantum left (6 units of burst left).
- 5–7 P3 (Q0, full, 1 left) → Q1 = [P1, P2, P3].
- 7–10 P1 uses the remaining 3 units of its quantum → quantum exhausted with 3 left → demoted to Q2.
- 10–14 **P2** (Q1, 4 left, quantum 4) → finishes exactly at **14** (no demotion).
- 14–15 P3 (done). 15–18 P1 in Q2 (done).

Gantt chart:
```
| P1 | P2 | P1 | P3 | P1 | P2 | P3 | P1 |
0    2    4    5    7    10   14   15   18
```
questions.trap: Giving P1 a fresh 4-unit quantum at 7 (P2 then finishes at 15), or sending P1 to the tail of Q1 (the other common rule; P2 would finish at 11).

questions.stem:
An MLFQ has Q0 (RR, quantum 4), Q1 (RR, quantum 8) and Q2 (FCFS). Rules:
- New processes enter the tail of Q0.
- A process that uses its full quantum without finishing moves to the tail of the next lower queue.
- A process arriving in a higher queue immediately preempts a process running from a lower queue; the preempted process goes to the **tail of its own queue** and receives a fresh quantum when next dispatched.
- A lower queue runs only when all higher queues are empty. Ignore switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 30 |
| P2 | 5 | 10 |
| P3 | 14 | 4 |
| P4 | a | 7 |

a is an integer with 20 ≤ a ≤ 40. The **smallest** a for which P4's turnaround time is **less than 10** is ______.
questions.explanation:
**Schedule before P4 arrives** (same for every a ≥ 20):
- 0–4 P1 (Q0, full) → Q1; 4–5 P1 from Q1, preempted by P2 → tail of Q1.
- 5–9 P2 (Q0, full, 6 left) → Q1 = [P1, P2].
- 9–14 P1 (Q1), preempted by P3 → Q1 = [P2, P1].
- 14–18 P3 (Q0, finishes exactly at quantum end).
- 18–24 P2 from Q1 (6 left, done at 24).
- 24–32 P1 from Q1 with a fresh quantum 8 → uses it fully → **demoted to Q2 at 32** (12 left).

P4 needs 4 units in Q0, is then demoted, and needs 3 more in Q1. TAT < 10 requires those 3 units to run right after its Q0 quantum, i.e. **no Q1 process ahead of it**.

- 20 ≤ a ≤ 23: P2 is running in Q1 → P2 goes to the tail of Q1 behind P1; P4 then queues behind both → TAT 16–19.
- a = 24: P4 runs 24–28, then waits behind P1 in Q1 (P1 28–36) → P4 36–39, TAT 15.
- 25 ≤ a ≤ 31: P4 preempts P1, which goes to the tail of Q1 **with a fresh 8-unit quantum**; P4 lands behind it → CT = a + 4 + 8 + 3 → TAT 15.
- **a = 32:** P1 has just been demoted to Q2. P4 runs 32–36 in Q0, then 36–39 in Q1 (Q1 holds only P4) → TAT **7**.
- a ≥ 32 behaves the same way (P1 is in Q2).

Smallest a = **32**.
questions.trap: Assuming that arriving later always hurts P4, or forgetting that a preempted Q1 process gets a fresh quantum, so P1 keeps occupying Q1 until exactly 32.

questions.stem:
Four processes must be run **non-preemptively** on one CPU (once started, a process runs to completion). The scheduler knows all arrival times and bursts in advance and is allowed to leave the CPU idle deliberately even when a process is ready. Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 6 |
| P2 | 1 | 1 |
| P3 | 2 | 3 |
| P4 | 3 | 1 |

The minimum possible average waiting time over all such non-preemptive schedules is ______ (correct to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
For a fixed execution order, starting each process as early as possible is best, so we only need to compare orders.

**P1 first (greedy, what non-preemptive SJF does):** P1 0–6; then P2, P4, P3 are all waiting: P2 6–7, P4 7–8, P3 8–11 → WT = 0 + 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 (avg 3.75).

**P1 in the middle:** some short job waits behind its 6 units. The best such orders are P2, P4, P1, P3 (WT 0 + 0 + 4 + 8 = 12) and P2, P3, P1, P4 (WT 0 + 0 + 5 + 8 = 13) — all ≥ 12.

**P1 last:** idle 0–1 (deliberately), then the three short jobs, then P1.
- P2 1–2, P3 2–5, P4 5–6, P1 6–12 → WT: P2 0, P3 0, P4 2, P1 6 → **8**.
- P2 1–2, idle 2–3, P4 3–4, P3 4–7, P1 7–13 → WT 0 + 2 + 0 + 7 = 9.

Lower bound for this case: the short jobs need 5 units of CPU and the first cannot start before 1, so P1 cannot start before 6 (WT ≥ 6), and P3 and P4 cannot both start on arrival (they overlap at 3), so at least 2 more units of waiting arise either on P4 (2) or on P3 plus a later P1.

Minimum total WT = 8 → average = 8 / 4 = **2.00**.

(Compare: non-preemptive SJF 3.75; preemptive SRTF would reach 1.5, but preemption is not allowed.)
questions.trap: Assuming non-preemptive SJF is optimal (3.75): with staggered arrivals, idling for 1 unit to avoid starting the long job is better. Using SRTF (1.50) violates the non-preemptive constraint.

questions.stem:
Three processes are scheduled FCFS on one CPU (a process returning from I/O joins the tail of the ready queue; if two processes join the ready queue at the same instant, the lower-numbered one is queued first). Each process has its own I/O device. Ignore context-switch time.

| Process | Arrival | CPU | I/O | CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 4 | y | 3 |
| P2 | 1 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| P3 | 2 | 5 | — | — |

Let T(y) be the average turnaround time. For how many integer values of y with 1 ≤ y ≤ 15 is **T(y) < T(1)**?
questions.explanation:
The first part of the schedule does not depend on y:
```
| P1 | P2 | P3 |
0    4    7    12
```
P3 finishes at 12 (TAT 10). P2 does I/O 7–9 and is ready at 9. P1 does I/O 4 → 4 + y and is ready at 4 + y.

**Case 1: 4 + y ≤ 9 (y ≤ 5).** P1 is queued before P2 (at y = 5 both join at 9 and P1 wins on index). P1 12–15, P2 15–17 → TAT 15 + 16 + 10 = 41.

**Case 2: 9 < 4 + y ≤ 14 (6 ≤ y ≤ 10).** P2 is ahead: P2 12–14, P1 runs from 14 → 17 → TAT 17 + 13 + 10 = 40.

**Case 3: 4 + y > 14 (y ≥ 11).** P2 12–14, CPU idles until P1 returns at 4 + y, P1 ends at 7 + y → TAT (7 + y) + 13 + 10 = 30 + y ≥ 41.

So T(1) = 41/3, and T(y) < T(1) exactly for y = 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 → **5** values.

The counter-intuitive part: a *longer* I/O for P1 lowers the average, because it lets the short second burst of P2 go first (an SJF-like effect).
questions.trap: Assuming T(y) can only grow with y (answer 0), giving the tie at y = 5 to P2, or counting y = 11 where T equals T(1) rather than being smaller.

questions.stem:
An MLFQ has Q0 (RR, quantum 4), Q1 (RR, quantum 8) and Q2 (FCFS). Rules:
- New processes enter the tail of Q0. A process that uses its full quantum without finishing its current CPU burst moves to the tail of the next lower queue.
- A process that blocks for I/O before its quantum expires stays in the same queue and rejoins its tail (fresh quantum) when the I/O completes.
- A process becoming ready in a higher queue immediately preempts a process running from a lower queue; the preempted process goes to the tail of its own queue with a fresh quantum.
- Each process has its own I/O device; ignore switch time.

Process A (CPU-bound, single burst of 20) arrives at time 0. Process B arrives at time 0 just after A and needs 15 units of CPU in total, with a 1-unit I/O after every CPU burst except the last. Consider two versions of B:
- **Version 1:** five CPU bursts of 3 units each.
- **Version 2:** three CPU bursts of 5 units each.

B's completion time in version 2 minus its completion time in version 1 is ______.
questions.explanation:
**Version 1 (bursts of 3 < quantum 4: B never gets demoted).**
- 0–4 A (full quantum) → Q1.
- 4–7 B, blocks (stays in Q0); I/O 7–8. A runs 7–8 from Q1; at 8 B returns to Q0 and preempts A (A to the tail of Q1, fresh quantum).
- The pattern repeats every 4 units: B 8–11, A 11–12, B 12–15, A 15–16, B 16–19, A 19–20, B 20–23 (done).
```
| A | B | A | B | A | B | A | B | A | B | A |
0   4   7   8   11  12  15  16  19  20  23  35
```
B completes at **23**. A never gets 8 consecutive units in Q1 while B is around.

**Version 2 (bursts of 5 > quantum 4).**
- 0–4 A → Q1. 4–8 B uses its full quantum (1 unit of the burst left) → demoted to Q1 = [A, B].
- 8–16 A (Q1, full quantum) → Q2 (8 left).
- 16–17 B finishes its first burst in Q1; I/O 17–18 (stays in Q1). A runs 17–18 from Q2.
- 18–23 B (Q1, 5 < 8), I/O 23–24; A 23–24. 24–29 B (done). A 29–35.
```
| A | B | A | B | A | B | A | B | A |
0   4   8   16  17  18  23  24  29  35
```
B completes at **29**.

Difference = 29 − 23 = **6**. Splitting the same CPU demand into bursts shorter than the Q0 quantum keeps B in the top queue — the classic way a process can game an MLFQ that resets its quantum on every I/O.
questions.trap: Demoting version-1 B because its total CPU (15) exceeds the quantum, or letting version-2 B finish its 5-unit burst in Q0.
